title: Lab: GRPO from scratch on Tiny Adder
summary: Build a complete GRPO trainer in under 100 lines of numpy and teach a lookup-table model to add, using only right/wrong verdicts. Then swap in a buggy grader and watch reward hacking happen.
learningObjectives: Implement one GRPO step: group sampling, normalized advantages and the REINFORCE nudge with a group baseline
Add optional clipping over several inner steps and a KL pull toward a reference
Read a training log of reward, accuracy and entropy and explain the slow start and S-curve
Recognize reward hacking when reward rises but true accuracy stays flat

studyGuide.mentalModel: A table of 100 rows (one per sum) by 19 columns (one per answer), all zeros at the start. Each step, ask 16 questions, take 8 guesses each, grade them, and shift each row's scores toward the guesses that beat their group's average. A grader that pays for the wrong thing gets exactly what it pays for.
keyIdeas: One GRPO step = sample a batch, sample a group per prompt, grade, normalize within the group, nudge.
The nudge onehot(k) - softmax(L) raises the sampled answer and lowers the rest in proportion to their probability.
With ppo_epochs = 1 the ratio is 1 and clipping never fires; the update is plain REINFORCE with a group baseline.
The slow start comes from silent all-wrong groups; once a few right answers appear, a feedback loop gives an S-curve.
Reward is measured by the grader, accuracy by the truth. When they split, suspect the grader.
misconceptions: A flat first stretch is not automatically failure; check whether any groups have non-zero reward spread.
Falling entropy is not always collapse; here it falls because the model becomes confidently right.
A rising reward curve does not prove the model learned the task; the buggy grader's reward rises while accuracy stays at chance.
The toy's exact numbers depend on the random seed and implementation; the shapes are what transfer.
recallPrompts: List the five things that happen in one GRPO training step.
Why does the honest run barely improve for the first 50 steps?
In the buggy run, why does reward start near 0.55 instead of 0.05?
Which logged number would reveal reward hacking, and why?
studyGuide.explainBackPrompt: Explain to a friend how a table of numbers can learn to add from nothing but right/wrong feedback, and how a badly written grader can make it look like it learned when it did not.

quiz.prompt: All Tiny Adder logits start at zero. What is the model's accuracy before any training?
quiz.explanation: Zero logits mean a uniform distribution over 19 answers, so each guess is right with probability 1/19, about 0.05.

quiz.prompt: In the healthy run, reward stays near 0.1 for about the first 50 steps. Why?
options: The learning rate warms up slowly by design
The reward function only switches on after step 50
Most groups of 8 random guesses contain no right answer, so their advantages are zero and they teach nothing
quiz.explanation: With 1-in-19 guesses, about 65% of groups are all wrong. Only the lucky groups produce a learning signal until right answers become more common.

quiz.prompt: In the update ratio * A * (onehot(k) - p_new), what does (onehot(k) - p_new) do when A is positive?
options: Raises the score of the sampled answer k and lowers the others in proportion to their probability
Copies the true sum into the table
quiz.explanation: onehot(k) has a 1 at k, and subtracting the current probabilities lowers every answer a little, so the sampled answer gains relative to the rest.

quiz.prompt: With buggy=True, reward climbs to about 0.81 by step 200. Which observation proves the model has not learned addition?
options: Accuracy against the true sum stays at about 0.05, pure chance
quiz.explanation: Accuracy is measured against the truth, not the grader. Flat accuracy with rising reward is the signature of reward hacking.

quiz.prompt: With the default ppo_epochs = 1, what does clipping do in grpo_tiny_adder.py?
options: Nothing: the ratio is exactly 1 on the only inner step, so no answer is ever clipped
quiz.explanation: The ratio compares the current policy with the one that sampled the answers. On the first (and only) inner step they are identical, so ratio = 1, which is always inside the band.

exercises.title: How big should the group be?
hints: Call train(G=g) for g in 2, 4, 8, 16 and read the last history entry.
Also find the first step where accuracy passes 0.5.
Think about cost: each step samples batch x G answers.

exercises.title: Write a grader that is harder to hack
hints: The buggy grader ignores a and b. Any honest grader must use them.
Try partial credit: 1 for the exact sum, 0.5 for being off by one.
Check both reward and accuracy: does partial credit help the slow start?
